summary: Students learn the life cycle of a star as a narrative of change driven by two competing agents — gravity pulling inward and the outward pressure of energy from fusion — with the star's initial MASS deciding its whole fate. The Sun-like path runs nebula → protostar → main sequence (long, stable phase where hydrogen fuses to helium and gravity is balanced by fusion pressure) → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf. Massive stars burn brighter and shorter and end violently: red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole. The payoff is nucleosynthesis: fusion inside stars forges elements up to iron; the heaviest elements are forged in extreme events such as supernovae and neutron-star collisions, with some made in ageing giant stars; and dying stars scatter this enriched material to seed the clouds that form the next generation of stars and planets — so most of the atoms in our bodies, apart from hydrogen, were made in stars. Because a star's life spans millions to billions of years, we read the cycle not by watching one star but by observing many stars at different stages — an evidence-and-inference move worth making explicit. Aimed at ages 13–14, anchored on NGSS HS-ESS1-3.
misconceptions: All stars end the same way / follow one linear path regardless of mass (mass determines whether the end is a white dwarf or a supernova remnant)
Stars are on fire / burn like combustion rather than releasing energy by nuclear fusion
A supernova is the star burning out quietly, or a black hole 'sucks in' everything nearby like a vacuum (it is the extreme gravity of a collapsed massive core)
Stars last forever or are unchanging; or the Sun will explode as a supernova (the Sun is too low-mass — it will become a red giant then a white dwarf)
The heavy elements always existed / elements are not made in stars (fusion and supernovae are where elements heavier than hydrogen/helium originate)
A 'nebula' is only a birthplace (planetary nebulae are also produced at a star's death), and a planetary nebula has to do with planets (it does not)

activities.title: Build-a-star: one dial, two very different deaths
steps: Set a 'mass dial' (or choose a mass card) for a newborn star to LOW/Sun-like, predict out loud what will happen over its life, then run the life cycle and watch it unfold stage by stage: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf.

At each stage, read a gravity-vs-pressure balance indicator (inward arrows vs outward arrows, or a simple meter): watch contraction heat the core until fusion ignites, balance hold steady through the long main sequence, then the balance tip as fuel falters.

Reset the dial to HIGH mass, predict again, and re-run, keeping everything else in the model the same: watch the more massive newborn star (formed from a bigger collapsing clump of gas) blaze faster, bloat into a supergiant, and explode as a supernova leaving a neutron star or black hole.

Watch an element ticker (a running count of nuclei forged) build heavier elements through the star's life (up to about carbon and oxygen in the low-mass run, up to iron in the high-mass core), then see the low-mass star shed enriched gas as a planetary nebula and, in the high-mass run, see the supernova fling material out to seed the next cloud.
State in one sentence what single thing the student changed between the two runs, and what it decided.
activities.insight: A star's initial mass decides its whole fate: a low-mass star ends as a quiet white dwarf, while a high-mass star ends in a supernova that leaves a neutron star or black hole. The stable main sequence is gravity balanced by fusion pressure, and each later stage is that balance being lost. Elements heavier than hydrogen and helium are forged inside stars and returned to space, gently by dying low-mass stars and violently by supernovae.

activities.title: Explore each stage: lift-the-flap branching diagram
steps: Work along a branching life-cycle diagram keyed on mass: low/medium mass → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf; high mass → supergiant → supernova → neutron star / black hole.

Tap or lift a flap at each node (nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant/supergiant, planetary nebula/supernova, end state) to reveal: what is happening, the gravity/fusion balance state, and the element story.
Drill down from 'supernova' into the fact that many of the heaviest elements are forged and scattered there (others come from neutron-star collisions and ageing giant stars).
Trace both the Sun-like path and the massive-star path with a finger and say where they diverge and why.
Distinguish on the diagram: a star vs a planet vs the initial cloud; and note that 'nebula' appears as both a birthplace and (planetary nebula) a death product.
activities.insight: The cycle is a well-defined sequence of named stages, and mass determines which of two labelled branches a star follows. The terms 'nebula' and 'planetary nebula' name different things.

activities.title: Reading the sky: inferring a life cycle from a snapshot
steps: Discuss why we cannot watch one star live and die (a star's life spans millions to billions of years — far longer than human history).
Given a 'crowd photo' of many stars caught at different stages, sort them into life-cycle stages and argue which stage each is in.
Explain, in your own words, how observing many stars at different stages lets us infer the whole life cycle — comparing it to inferring a human life cycle from one photo of a crowd of different ages.
Optionally place stages on a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram at an introductory level to see where the main sequence and later stages sit.
activities.insight: Because stars live far longer than we can observe, scientists infer the life cycle by observing a population of stars at different stages — an explicit evidence-and-inference move.

activities.title: In role with an astrophysicist: wonder and misconceptions
steps: Pose questions to an astrophysicist character (teacher-in-role, scripted dialogue, or peers): 'How will the Sun die?', 'Where did the gold in a ring come from?', 'Where did the iron in my blood come from?'
Challenge claims Socratically: if a star is 'on fire', where does the energy really come from? If everything was made in the Big Bang, how did we get carbon and iron?
Summarise the 'we are star stuff' idea in your own words after the discussion.
activities.insight: Elements heavier than hydrogen and helium were forged in stars and in stellar explosions and collisions, then scattered into space by dying stars, so most atoms in our bodies other than hydrogen were built in stars — and 'burning' means nuclear fusion, not chemical combustion.

activities.title: Check understanding: sequence, match, and diagnose
steps: Order the Sun-like stages: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf.
Match initial mass to end state: low/medium mass → white dwarf; high mass → neutron star or black hole.

Answer: where are elements heavier than hydrogen and helium made? (fusion in stars up to iron; heaviest in extreme events such as supernovae and neutron-star collisions, plus some in ageing giant stars).
Two-tier diagnostic: 'Two stars form at the same time: one like our Sun, one ten times more massive. Which runs out of fuel and dies first — and why?' Then give a reason.
Explain: a massive star has far more fuel than the Sun yet lives a far shorter life — how can both be true?
activities.insight: Students can sequence the stages, map mass to end state, and — crucially — reason that mass sets the burn RATE, so the more massive star dies first despite having more fuel.

checkQuestion: Two stars form at the same time: one like our Sun, and one ten times more massive. Which one runs out of fuel and dies first — and why?
checkAnswer: The MORE massive star dies first — in a few million years, versus billions for the Sun. Although it has more fuel, its far stronger gravity makes its core hotter and its fusion run enormously faster, so it burns through its fuel much sooner — and it ends in a supernova, while the Sun will not.
